bank.prompt: The black king is a file outside the box. Push.
bank.reason: Three moves for the pawn, four for the king on e7. Any other move gives Black the tempo it needs.

bank.prompt: Draw the box from b5 before you move. Then move.
bank.reason: The box is b5 to e5; the king is on f7, one file too far. b6 and the pawn is gone.

bank.prompt: Black to move. Hold the draw.
bank.reason: Kd6 puts the kings face to face with d5 between them, and White has to give way.

bank.prompt: Black to move. Stand in the pawn's path.
bank.reason: Ke6, directly opposite the white king on e4. White must move first and must step aside.

bank.prompt: Black to move, king on f6. Stop the pawn.
bank.reason: Ke6. Beside the enemy king is not enough — the defender's square is the one in front of the pawn.

bank.prompt: A pawn down on the h-file. Save it.
bank.reason: Kg8 and then Kh8. Reach the corner in front of the pawn and the position cannot be won.

bank.prompt: The pawn is on a5 and your king is on c8. Save it.
bank.reason: Kb8, heading for a8. Kd8 runs the wrong way and the pawn walks in.

bank.prompt: Both pawns are three moves from home and it is your turn.
bank.reason: Push. Equal counts go to the side to move, and one quiet move would hand that away.

bank.prompt: Your king already stands on the h-pawn's road. Get on with your own.
bank.reason: a6. The h-pawn reaches h3 and is taken, so there is nothing to defend and no reason to wait.

bank.prompt: The white king covers g7 and h7. Tap the square where the rook mates in one.
bank.reason: Ra8 seals the eighth rank while the king on g6 covers both escape squares.

bank.prompt: The pawn on a5 is three moves from home. Tap the far corner of its box on the fifth rank.
bank.reason: d5. Three files across from a5, because the pawn needs three moves.

bank.prompt: Tap the corner square the black king must reach to hold the draw.
bank.reason: h8 — the pawn's own queening square. A king sitting on it can never be evicted.

bank.prompt: Tap the corner square that saves Black here.
bank.reason: a8, in front of the pawn. The corner on the far side of the board is worth nothing.

bank.prompt: Tap the square where Black's king stands face to face with White's, one square between them.
bank.reason: d6, on the same file as d4 with d5 empty between. That stand-off is the draw.

bank.prompt: Tap White's passed pawn.
bank.reason: a2. Black has no pawn on the a-file or b-file, so that one can run if the king escorts it.

bank.prompt: Tap the square White's pawn is racing to.
bank.reason: a8, three pushes away — and Black's pawn needs three to reach h1, so the move decides it.

bank.prompt: Tap the square where the black king blocks the pawn and faces the white king.
bank.reason: e6. Same file as e4, one square between, and the pawn on e3 behind it can make no progress.

bank.prompt: Tap every white piece that could force mate with only the king to help.
bank.reason: The queen and the rook. Each can cut off a whole rank, which is what drives a king to the edge.

bank.prompt: Tap every white piece that could never force mate, however long the game went on.
bank.reason: The bishop and the knight. A bishop touches one colour only, and a lone knight is far too slow.

bank.prompt: Tap every square on the fifth rank inside the b5 pawn's box.
bank.reason: b5 to e5 — four squares wide, because the pawn needs three moves. f7 is outside it.

bank.prompt: The white king covers the seventh rank. Tap every square the black king may move to.
bank.reason: Only e8 and g8. Two choices, and one of them throws the draw away.

bank.prompt: Tap every square the white king on e1 can step to.
bank.reason: d1, d2, e2 and f1 — f2 is blocked by its own pawn. The useful ones head for the centre.

bank.prompt: Tap every square White's pawn still has to cross to reach the last rank.
bank.reason: a6, a7 and a8 — three moves. Count Black's the same way and the race answers itself.

bank.prompt: King and bishop against a bare king. What is the result with best play?
options: A draw — a lone bishop can never force mate.
White mates, but it takes around thirty moves.
White mates only if the black king strays to a light square.
bank.reason: Drawn from the start. Half the board is a colour the bishop can never touch.

bank.prompt: Two knights against a bare king. What is the honest verdict?
options: It cannot be forced — closing the net gives stalemate instead.
A routine mate, easier than king and rook.
Mate only if the knights sit on squares of the same colour.
bank.reason: It cannot be forced. Treat two knights against a bare king as a draw and play for something else.

bank.prompt: The same position as the h-pawn draw, but with the pawn on g5. Does Black still hold?
options: No. With a file beyond the pawn, White's king can push the defender out and win.
Yes — the defending king is close enough, whatever the file.
Yes, but only because it is Black to move.
bank.reason: White wins. The h-file gives the attacker room to outflank, which is exactly what an edge pawn lacks.

bank.prompt: Why can the defending king never be driven out of the corner here?
options: There is no file beyond the pawn, so the attacking king has nowhere to squeeze from.
A king in the corner cannot legally be checked.
An edge pawn is not permitted to promote to a queen.
bank.reason: The board runs out. Pushing a king off a square needs squares on both sides of it, and past the h-file there are none.

bank.prompt: Kings on d4 and d6, pawn on d3, White to move. Who is better off?
options: Black. White must step aside, and the black king stays in front of the pawn.
White — having the move is always worth something.
Neither; the kings are equally placed, so it is symmetrical.
bank.reason: Black holds. In this stand-off the side obliged to move is the side that gives ground.

bank.prompt: White's king is on d6, directly in front of its own pawn on d5. What is the verdict?
options: White wins, whoever is to move.
Drawn, because the black king sits on the queening file.
White wins only with Black to move.
bank.reason: Won either way. A king on the sixth rank ahead of its pawn can no longer be kept out.

bank.prompt: Both pawns need the same number of moves. What settles a tie like this?
options: The side to move arrives first.
The pawn closer to the edge of the board promotes first.
A tie means both promote and the game is drawn by rule.
bank.reason: Whoever is to move. That is why one quiet move is so expensive: it costs you the tie-break, not a pawn.

bank.prompt: For the whole game the king has been kept tucked away. Why does that change in an ending?
options: The pieces that could punish an exposed king have been traded, so the king becomes a fighting piece.
The rules let the king move further once most pieces are gone.
It does not change; the king belongs on the back rank to the end.
bank.reason: Nothing is left to check it. The same king that had to hide is now a piece worth about a knight and a half.

bank.prompt: White swings the bishop to h7, right beside the black king. Is it safe?
reasons: Yes — the black king cannot reach h7 from h8.
No. The king on h8 simply takes it.
No. It would be pinned against the white king.
bank.reason: Kxh7 and the board is bare. Nothing of White's defends h7, and a lone bishop has no helper to give it one.

bank.prompt: White marches the king to e4, into the open centre. Is it safe there?
reasons: Yes. Nothing Black has left can attack e4.
No. The pawn on f7 covers e4.
No. The black king on g8 defends the fourth rank.
bank.reason: Entirely safe. The f7 pawn hits e6 and g6, and with no queen or rook on the board there is nothing to fear.

bank.prompt: White starts the walk with Ke2. Is the king safe on e2?
reasons: Yes. Black has a king on g8 and three pawns, and none of them reaches e2.
No. The pawn on f7 attacks e2 down the file.
No. The black king can reach e2 in two moves.
bank.reason: Safe, and the first step of the journey. Black's nearest man is five squares away.

bank.prompt: White plays Kh3, attacking the pawn on h4. Is the king safe there?
reasons: Yes. A black pawn on h4 captures towards g3, not h3.
No. The pawn on h4 takes it.
No. The black king on e7 defends h4.
bank.reason: Safe. A pawn never captures straight down the file it stands on, so h4 cannot touch h3 — though pushing the a-pawn is still the stronger move.
